text.hook:
std::async, futures, thread_local, call_once: easy to use, easy to get wrong in an interview.

Here is the mental model, plus 6 myths that fail interviews. Save it. 📌
text.body:
Inside:
1. The shared state behind promise and future
2. The three launch policies of std::async
3. The blocking destructor trap
4. thread_local: one instance per thread
5. Once-only init: what actually works
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

first_comment: 🧠 Test yourself: can you call `get_future()` twice on the same std::promise? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. The second call throws `std::future_error` with code `future_already_retrieved`.

slides.lead: One-shot channels, launch policies, per-thread state and once-only init.

slides.title: A one-shot channel for a value or an exception

cards.label: Producer
cards.text: `promise`, `packaged_task`, or the `std::async` task. Writes the result **once**.

cards.label: Shared state
cards.text: Typically heap-allocated, reference-counted: value or `exception_ptr`, plus a ready flag.

slides.takeaway: `set_value` *synchronizes-with* the return of `get()`: data written before it is visible after.

slides.title: Three launch policies
rows: as if on a new `std::thread`, starts promptly, fresh `thread_local`s
runs on the thread that calls `get()`/`wait()`, and never otherwise

slides.title: This loop runs one task at a time
slides.code:
for (auto& item : items)
    std::async(std::launch::async, process, item);
bullets: The returned temporary future dies at the end of each statement.
The last future of an async-launched task **blocks in its destructor** until the task completes.
slides.tip: C++20 marks `std::async` `[[nodiscard]]`, so compilers warn. Keep the futures, or use a pool.
slides.takeaway: Futures from `promise` or `packaged_task` never block in their destructor.

slides.title: Say these precisely
items: `get()` waits for the **result**, not for the thread to exit
A `packaged_task` never runs by itself: someone must invoke it
slides.warn: A second `get()` on a `std::future` is UB. Many readers? Use `shared_future`.

slides.title: One instance per thread

cards.label: What it is
cards.text: Thread storage duration: each thread gets its own instance, destroyed when that thread exits.

cards.label: Where it lives
cards.text: In the thread's TLS block (`fs`-relative on x86-64 Linux). Not a stack variable.

cards.label: What it is not
cards.text: Synchronization. It removes sharing; it protects nothing that is shared.

slides.takeaway: Thread pools reuse threads: `thread_local` state from one task is still there for the next.

slides.title: What actually works
rows: none: data race (UB), init may run twice
no UB, but init may still run twice
thread-safe one-time construction, retry on throw
one successful run, waiting, publication, retry on throw
slides.takeaway: Magic static for one lazily built object. `call_once` for an arbitrary or per-object once.

items.myth: "`future.get()` waits for the thread to finish."
items.truth: It waits for the result to become ready. The producer may keep running.
Only `std::launch::async` guarantees it runs as if on a new thread. The default policy may defer.
Only the last future from a `std::async` launched task.

items.myth: "A destroyed promise leaves the future waiting forever."

items.truth: It removes sharing. It does not protect anything that is shared.

items.myth: "If the `call_once` function throws, the flag is consumed."
items.truth: The flag stays unset. The next call retries.

slides.hero:
future: a one-shot channel.
thread_local: no sharing.
call_once: elect, wait, publish.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
Three threads, one counter variable, 100 increments each. 🧵

No mutex, no atomic. What prints?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Read every line before you answer.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: a detached thread is still running when main returns. Do its thread_local destructors run? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No. Detached threads still running at process exit never get their thread_local destructors. For a joined thread they run at its exit, before join() returns.

slides.title: What does this print?

slides.verdict_sub: Each thread has its own `counter`. No data race.
bullets: `thread_local`: every thread gets its own `counter`, starting at 0.
Each instance is incremented 100 times by its own thread only.
`result[i]` are distinct objects, read after `join()`.
`main`'s own instance was never incremented.

slides.title: Same code, one keyword removed
slides.tip: Per-thread counters merged later avoid contention, but the merge itself needs synchronization.
slides.takeaway: thread_local is about which object a thread sees, not about synchronization.

text.hook:
"Fire and forget" with std::async. 🚀

The task sleeps 200 ms. In what order do the three lines print?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Read the call to std::async carefully. One line does more than it looks.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: someone "fixes" it with `for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) { auto f = std::async(std::launch::async, job); }`. Do the 4 jobs run in parallel? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: No, one after another. f is destroyed at the end of each iteration, and its destructor waits for that task. Keep all the futures alive, e.g. in a std::vector.

slides.title:
In what order do
the lines print?
options: Order varies from run to run

slides.verdict: B: start, task finished, after async
slides.verdict_sub: Every run. The call is synchronous.
bullets: `std::async` returns a temporary `std::future`, destroyed at the end of the full expression.
The last future of an async-launched task **blocks in its destructor** until the task completes.
So the 200 ms task finishes before `after async` is printed.

slides.title: Keep the future
slides.tip: C++20 marks `std::async` `[[nodiscard]]`: GCC warns when the result is ignored.
slides.takeaway: A discarded `std::async` future makes the call synchronous. Keep the future, or use a pool.

text.hook:
The producer thread finishes without ever setting the promise. 🤝

Does main hang forever in get()?
Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: A classic error-path bug. What the standard library does here is worth knowing by heart.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: what happens if `set_value` is called a second time on the same std::promise? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: It throws std::future_error with code promise_already_satisfied. Unlike a second get() on a std::future, this case is well defined.

slides.title:
The promise is never set.
What happens?

bullets: The promise was moved into the lambda, so it dies with the thread's callable when the lambda returns unset.
A promise destroyed without a result stores `future_error(broken_promise)` and makes the state ready.
`get()` wakes up and throws. No hang.
The `what()` text is libstdc++'s. Portable check: `e.code() == std::future_errc::broken_promise`.

slides.title: Broken is loud. Dangling is UB.

columns.label: By ref + detach

slides.takeaway: An abandoned promise breaks loudly. A dangling one is UB: move the promise into the thread.

text.hook:
One std::async per incoming message.
Clean, modern C++. It passed code review.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Think about what each call really does on Linux, not what the code looks like.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: how do GCC and Clang make the initialization of a function-local `static` thread-safe, and what does the fast path cost? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: A guard variable. Fast path: an acquire load of the guard byte and a branch. The first use goes through __cxa_guard_acquire/release, which lock, construct once and make other callers wait.

slides.title:
Called once per message.
What does each call cost?
options: A new thread + a heap alloc

slides.verdict: A. A new thread, every call
slides.verdict_sub: libstdc++ starts a new thread per `launch::async` call: about 15 µs each on one test machine
bullets: Plus a heap-allocated shared state, context switches and a cold cache.
No control over core affinity, priority, queue bounds or allocation.
`launch::async` runs the task now, on its own thread. It does not wait for `get()`.
The standard gives no performance guarantees. MSVC's pool still allocates.
slides.wrong: "async is cheap, the library optimizes it"

slides.title: Preallocated ring + one pinned worker
slides.tip: `std::async` is fine for coarse work: startup, batch jobs.
slides.takeaway: Convenient is not cheap: keep `std::async` off any path measured in microseconds.

text.hook:
Review flagged a data race on the init flag.
The fix: make it std::atomic<bool>. Done?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: The most common answer is only half right.

first_comment: 🧠 Bonus: double-checked locking with `std::atomic<T*> instance`. Which memory orders do the fast-path load and the publishing store need? Reply with your answer 👇 I'll post the answer here tomorrow.
bonus_answer: Acquire on the fast-path load, release on the store after construction. The recheck under the mutex may be relaxed. With a plain T* it is a data race.

slides.title:
`initialized` is atomic now.
Is this safe?

slides.verdict_sub: Atomic steps, non-atomic sequence. Test run, 8 threads, slow `init()`: "init ran 8 times"
bullets: T1 reads false, T2 reads false, both call `init()`, both set true.
`atomic` removed the UB. The check-then-act gap is still there.
With a plain `bool` it was also a data race: undefined behaviour.

slides.title: Let the library elect one initializer
slides.tip: `call_once` elects one executor, blocks the rest, publishes its writes, retries on exception. A function-local `static` works too.
slides.takeaway: Once-only init needs election, waiting and publication. That is exactly what `call_once` is.
